claim: Gyrase is a unique type IIA topoisomerase that uses ATP hydrolysis to maintain the negatively supercoiled state of bacterial DNA.
source: Gyrase is a unique type IIA topoisomerase that uses ATP hydrolysis to maintain the negatively supercoiled state of bacterial DNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the function of gyrase.

claim: Structures where the transported DNA molecule (T-segment) is trapped by the A subunit have not been observed prior to this study.
source: Structures where the transported DNA molecule (T-segment) is trapped by the A subunit have not been observed.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract as background context for the novelty of the current work.

claim: The cryoEM structures of two oligomeric complexes of open gyrase A dimers and DNA were determined.
source: Here we present the cryoEM structures of two oligomeric complexes of open gyrase A dimers and DNA.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The protein subunits in the Tetrahedral complex were solved to 4 Å resolution.
source: The protein subunits in these complexes were solved to 4 Å and 5.2 Å resolution.
evidence: Resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by FSC curves in supplementary figures.

claim: The protein subunits in the Dihedral complex were solved to 5.2 Å resolution.
source: The protein subunits in these complexes were solved to 4 Å and 5.2 Å resolution.
evidence: Resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by FSC curves in supplementary figures.

claim: One of the complexes traps a linear DNA molecule, a putative T-segment, which interacts with the open gyrase A dimers in two states.
source: One of the complexes traps a linear DNA molecule, a putative T-segment, which interacts with the open gyrase A dimers in two states, representing steps either prior to or after passage through the DNA-gate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: DNA topoisomerases are present in all three domains of life.
source: DNA topoisomerases are versatile enzymes that modify the topology of DNA and are present in all three domains of life (Schoeffler and Berger, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schoeffler and Berger, 2008.

claim: Type II topoisomerases change the linking number strictly in steps of two.
source: Whereas all type II topoisomerases change the linking number strictly in steps of two, type I enzymes can change the linking number in steps of one (type IA) or any number (type IB and IC).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about topoisomerase mechanisms.

claim: Type I enzymes can change the linking number in steps of one (type IA) or any number (type IB and IC).
source: Whereas all type II topoisomerases change the linking number strictly in steps of two, type I enzymes can change the linking number in steps of one (type IA) or any number (type IB and IC).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about topoisomerase mechanisms.

claim: Breaking the DNA phosphodiester backbone involves a transient phospho-tyrosine bond in all topoisomerases.
source: In all cases, breaking the DNA phosphodiester backbone involves a transient phospho-tyrosine bond.
evidence: This is a statement of established mechanistic knowledge.

claim: Type IA and type IIA enzymes show structural and sequence similarities.
source: All members of the same sub-type show structural and sequence similarities, but there are also clear similarities between type IA and type IIA enzymes, as both use an enzyme-bridged strand passage mechanism, break/religate the DNA in similar manner, and show common structural domains (Schoeffler and Berger, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Schoeffler and Berger, 2008.

claim: Topoisomerases are important targets for antibiotics and chemotherapeutics.
source: Due to their critical role in the cell, topoisomerases are important targets for antibiotics and chemotherapeutics (Collin et al., 2011; Pommier et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Collin et al., 2011 and Pommier et al., 2010.

claim: DNA gyrases are found in bacteria, archaea, and some eukaryotes (plants and plasmodial parasites).
source: DNA gyrases are type IIA topoisomerases found in bacteria, archaea, and some eukaryotes (plants [Evans-Roberts et al., 2016] and plasmodial parasites [Dar et al., 2007])
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Evans-Roberts et al., 2016 and Dar et al., 2007.

claim: Gyrase is capable of relaxing positive supercoils and introducing negative supercoils into DNA.
source: DNA gyrases are type IIA topoisomerases found in bacteria, archaea, and some eukaryotes (plants [Evans-Roberts et al., 2016] and plasmodial parasites [Dar et al., 2007]) and are capable of relaxing positive supercoils and introducing negative supercoils into DNA as well as performing other topological manipulations (Reece and Maxwell, 1991b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Reece and Maxwell, 1991b.

claim: Gyrase is an A2B2 heterotetramer formed by two GyrA and two GyrB subunits.
source: Unlike eukaryotic type IIA enzymes, which are large homodimers, gyrase is an A2B2 heterotetramer formed by two GyrA and two GyrB subunits (Mizuuchi et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Mizuuchi et al., 1978.

claim: Introduction of negative supercoils into DNA is a unique function of gyrase.
source: Introduction of negative supercoils into DNA is a unique function of gyrase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about gyrase function.

claim: The C-terminal domains (CTDs) of the GyrA subunits are involved in binding and guiding the DNA through the negative supercoiling cycle.
source: It is coupled to ATP hydrolysis and requires the C-terminal domains (CTDs) of the GyrA subunits, which are involved in binding and guiding the DNA through the negative supercoiling cycle (Lanz and Klostermeier, 2011; Lanz and Klostermeier, 2012; Reece and Maxwell, 1991a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lanz and Klostermeier, 2011; Lanz and Klostermeier, 2012; Reece and Maxwell, 1991a.

claim: Removal of the GyrA CTD abolishes the ability of gyrase to negatively supercoil DNA.
source: Removal of the GyrA CTD abolishes the ability of gyrase to negatively supercoil DNA, but the truncated enzyme can relax both negative and positive supercoils, similarly to other type IIA topoisomerases (Kampranis and Maxwell, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kampranis and Maxwell, 1996.

claim: The GyrA dimer forms two gates that facilitate DNA passage: the DNA gate and the C-gate.
source: The GyrA dimer forms two gates that facilitate DNA passage. One gate (DNA gate) binds DNA (G-segment) at the beginning of the cycle and cleaves the DNA using its conserved, catalytic tyrosines. The second gate (C-gate) opens later in the cycle to release the transported DNA segment (T-segment).
evidence: This is stated as part of the mechanistic description in the introduction.

claim: GyrB contains an ATPase domain and the GyrB dimer forms the N-gate.
source: GyrB contains an ATPase domain and the GyrB dimer forms the third of the gyrase gates (N-gate).
evidence: This is stated as part of the mechanistic description in the introduction.

claim: Low resolution EM structures provide understanding of gyrase global subunit arrangement and relative GyrA and GyrB positions.
source: Our understanding of gyrase global subunit arrangement and relative GyrA and GyrB positions comes from low resolution EM structures (Papillon et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Papillon et al., 2013.

claim: The most commonly crystallized gyrase fragment consists of a GyrA dimer with truncated CTDs, the C-terminal region of GyrB, and a short G-segment DNA bound and stabilized by a quinolone antibiotic.
source: The most commonly crystallized gyrase fragment consists of a GyrA dimer with truncated CTDs (GyrA-ΔCTD), the C-terminal region of GyrB, and a short G-segment DNA bound and stabilized by a quinolone antibiotic (for example Bax et al., 2010 and Blower et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bax et al., 2010 and Blower et al., 2016.

claim: Open conformations of a GyrA truncated dimer with different extents of DNA-gate opening have been observed in the absence of DNA.
source: Open conformations of a GyrA truncated dimer with different extents of DNA-gate opening have been observed (Rudolph and Klostermeier, 2013) in the absence of DNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Rudolph and Klostermeier, 2013.

claim: A structure of a fragment of human topoisomerase II spanning the region corresponding to the GyrA-ΔCTD and the TOPRIM domain of GyrB in complex with G-segment DNA was reported.
source: Recently, a structure of a fragment of human topoisomerase II spanning the region corresponding to the GyrA-ΔCTD and the TOPRIM domain of GyrB in complex with G-segment DNA was also reported (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: A structure of GyrB in complex with a putative T-segment has been reported recently.
source: A structure of GyrB in complex with a putative T-segment has been reported recently (Laponogov et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Laponogov et al., 2018.

claim: Structures where GyrA or the equivalent region in a type II topoisomerase interact with the T-segment have not been observed prior to this study.
source: but structures where GyrA or the equivalent region in a type II topoisomerase interact with the T-segment have not been observed, even though they are critical to understand the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This statement establishes the novelty of the current work by noting the absence of prior structures.

claim: The Dihedral complex is formed by four dimers assembled around linear B-DNA with D2 symmetry.
source: One of the oligomers is formed by four dimers assembled around linear B-DNA. The protein subunits in this oligomer are arranged with D2 symmetry, however, trapped DNA breaks the overall symmetry of the complex.
evidence: This is a description of the structure determined in this study.

claim: In the Dihedral complex, the GyrA-ΔCTD open dimers make two types of interactions with DNA, mimicking a T-segment either prior to entering or just after passing through the DNA-gate.
source: In this complex, the GyrA-ΔCTD open dimers make two types of interactions with DNA, mimicking a T-segment either prior to entering or just after passing through the DNA-gate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data presented in the study.

claim: The Tetrahedral complex has tetrahedral symmetry and is composed of six open dimers that trap a tightly bent DNA inside the complex.
source: The second complex has tetrahedral symmetry and is composed of six open dimers that trap a tightly bent DNA inside the complex.
evidence: This is a description of the structure determined in this study.

claim: In both structures the DNA is interacting with positively charged protein regions close to the DNA-gate.
source: In both structures the DNA is interacting with positively charged protein regions close to the DNA-gate.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The structures correspond to and support protein and DNA orientations predicted but not previously observed that are part of the catalytic cycle.
source: The structures correspond to and support protein and DNA orientations predicted (Chen et al., 2018; Gubaev and Klostermeier, 2014; Kampranis et al., 1999), but not previously observed, that are part of the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This statement connects the current findings to prior predictions supported by citations.

claim: The Dihedral complex was obtained by mixing GyrA-ΔCTD with 44 bp oligonucleotide and ciprofloxacin.
source: The Dihedral complex, built from four GyrA-ΔCTD open dimers, was obtained by mixing GyrA-ΔCTD with 44 bp oligonucleotide and ciprofloxacin.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for complex formation.

claim: The Tetrahedral complex was formed by mixing GyrA-ΔCTD, GyrB, and the oligonucleotide in the presence of ciprofloxacin and novobiocin.
source: The Tetrahedral complex, built from six GyrA-ΔCTD open dimers, was formed by mixing GyrA-ΔCTD, GyrB, and the oligonucleotide in the presence of ciprofloxacin and novobiocin.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for complex formation.

claim: When GyrB is excluded from the mixture, predominantly the Dihedral complex is obtained.
source: However, when GyrB is excluded from the mixture, predominantly the Dihedral complex is obtained, suggesting that GyrB facilitates the formation of the Tetrahedral complex.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The complexes formed in the presence or absence of glutaraldehyde and the antibiotics.
source: Importantly, the complexes formed in the presence or absence of glutaraldehyde and the antibiotics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which shows conclusively that the oligomers do not require crosslinking or antibiotics for formation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by figure reference.

claim: The Dihedral complex is formed by four dimers of GyrA-ΔCTD in the open conformation and linear DNA threading through the dimers.
source: CryoEM analysis showed that the complex is formed by four dimers of GyrA-ΔCTD in the open conformation and linear DNA threading through the dimers.
evidence: This is a description of the structure determined by cryoEM.

claim: Maps calculated with the DNA subtracted and with D2 symmetry achieved a higher resolution for the protein parts of the assembly (5.2 Å).
source: Maps calculated with the DNA subtracted and with D2 symmetry achieved a higher resolution for the protein parts of the assembly (5.2 Å) (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the resolution achieved in the reconstruction, supported by figures.

claim: Maps calculated without masking the DNA and with C1 symmetry extended to 7 Å resolution and showed a single, B-DNA molecule running across the center of the complex.
source: Furthermore, maps calculated without masking the DNA and with C1 symmetry extended to 7 Å resolution and showed a single, B-DNA molecule running across the center of the complex.
evidence: This describes the resolution and features of a different reconstruction.

claim: Maps calculated imposing C2 symmetry for the fully occupied particles extended to 6.35 Å resolution.
source: Maps calculated imposing C2 symmetry for the fully occupied particles extended to 6.35 Å resolution (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the resolution achieved for a specific subset of particles.

claim: At 6.35 Å resolution, the DNA was easily built as the density showed major and minor grooves, and even bumps for the phosphates in the backbone.
source: At this resolution, the DNA was easily built as the density showed major and minor grooves, and even bumps for the phosphates in the backbone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map for DNA.

claim: A low resolution cryoEM reconstruction of the Dihedral complex in the absence of antibiotics or crosslinkers shows the presence of DNA with the same path.
source: In addition, a low resolution cryoEM reconstruction of the Dihedral complex in the absence of antibiotics or crosslinkers shows the presence of DNA with the same path, further confirming that the DNA in the complex is not a result of crosslinking. (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by figure reference.

claim: The GyrA-ΔCTD monomer is composed of five domains: C-gate, coiled coil, tower, WHD and N-terminal tail.
source: The GyrA-ΔCTD monomer is composed of five domains: C-gate, coiled coil, tower, WHD and N-terminal tail (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the domain organization of the protein.

claim: The WHD domains form the DNA-gate and contain the catalytic tyrosines that cleave double stranded DNA.
source: The WHD domains form the DNA-gate and contain the catalytic tyrosines that cleave double stranded DNA.
evidence: This describes the functional role of the WHD domain.

claim: The tower domain helps stabilize the G-segment of DNA in the closed conformation of the GyrA dimer.
source: The tower domain sits adjacent to the WHD domain and is built by β-sheets and helices connected by loops. The tower domain helps stabilize the G-segment of DNA in the closed conformation of the GyrA dimer (Dong and Berger, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Dong and Berger, 2007.

claim: The interactions between dimers in the Dihedral complex are mediated mainly by contacts between the N-terminal tail of a monomer with the N-terminal tails and WHD domains of adjacent dimers as well as WHD-WHD and WHD-tower domain interactions.
source: The interactions between dimers in the Dihedral complex are mediated mainly by contacts between the N-terminal tail of a monomer with the N-terminal tails and WHD domains of adjacent dimers as well as WHD-WHD and WHD-tower domain interactions.
evidence: This describes the protein-protein interactions observed in the structure.

claim: Each dimer interacts with DNA trapped inside the complex and those interactions are mediated by arginines and lysines from the tower, WHD, C-gate domains as well as the coiled coil close to the C-gate.
source: Each dimer interacts with DNA trapped inside the complex and those interactions are mediated by arginines and lysines from the tower, WHD, C-gate domains as well as the coiled coil close to the C-gate.
evidence: This describes the protein-DNA interactions observed in the structure.

claim: The Tetrahedral complex reconstruction with imposed tetrahedral symmetry achieved a resolution of 4.0 Å.
source: Collecting tilted and untilted particles (673,694 particles), imposing tetrahedral symmetry, and masking out the central density improved the resolution to 4.0 Å (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2,Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the resolution achieved in the reconstruction.

claim: The final map of the Tetrahedral complex consists of 12 GyrA-ΔCTD monomers related to one another by tetrahedral symmetry.
source: The final map consists of 12 GyrA-ΔCTD monomers related to one another by tetrahedral symmetry.
evidence: This describes the composition and symmetry of the structure.

claim: The conformation of GyrA-ΔCTD dimers in the Tetrahedral complex is similar to the conformation of the widely open GyrA-ΔCTD dimer observed previously in the crystal structure of Bacillus subtilis GyrA-ΔCTD.
source: The conformation of GyrA-ΔCTD dimers in this complex is similar to the conformation of the widely open GyrA-ΔCTD dimer observed previously in the crystal structure of Bacillus subtilis GyrA-ΔCTD (Rudolph and Klostermeier, 2013) (PDB ID 4DDQ).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure, supported by citation.

claim: In the Tetrahedral assembly, GyrA dimers are situated at the two-fold axes of the complex and make contacts at the C-gate domains.
source: In the assembly, GyrA dimers are situated at the two-fold axes of the complex and make contacts at the C-gate domains, whereas the interactions between neighboring dimers at the three-fold axes involve contacts between the N-terminal tails as well as interactions between the N-terminal tails and adjacent tower and WHD domains.
evidence: This describes the protein-protein interactions in the structure.

claim: In the Tetrahedral complex models where no symmetry was imposed to visualize the DNA, the interactions between the protein and the DNA are mainly mediated by residues in the vicinity of the catalytic tyrosine as well as arginines in the tower domain.
source: In all models where no symmetry was imposed to visualize the DNA, the interactions between the protein and the DNA are mainly mediated by residues in the vicinity of the catalytic tyrosine as well as arginines in the tower domain.
evidence: This describes the protein-DNA interactions observed in the structure.

claim: Comparisons of the open dimers from the Tetrahedral and Dihedral complexes with the closed dimer from the crystal structure of S. pneumoniae dimer show rearrangements of the protein domains and subunits.
source: Comparisons of the open dimers from the Tetrahedral and Dihedral complexes with the closed dimer from the crystal structure of S. pneumoniae dimer (PDB ID 4Z2C) show rearrangements of the protein domains and subunits (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural comparison described in the results.

claim: The Tetrahedral dimer monomers are related to each other by the point group symmetry.
source: Interestingly, whereas the Tetrahedral dimer monomers are related to each other by the point group symmetry, the Dihedral dimer monomers are not related by the point group symmetry and hence are different (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation about the symmetry relationships in the structures.

claim: The Dihedral dimer monomers are not related by the point group symmetry and hence are different.
source: Interestingly, whereas the Tetrahedral dimer monomers are related to each other by the point group symmetry, the Dihedral dimer monomers are not related by the point group symmetry and hence are different (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation about the symmetry relationships in the structures.

claim: The comparisons show that every domain in the protein changes its relative position, which contributes to the overall conformational change.
source: The comparisons show that every domain in the protein changes its relative position, which contributes to the overall conformational change.
evidence: This is a conclusion from structural comparisons.

claim: The transition from the closed to the open state requires relative rearrangements of every GyrA domain and not a unidirectional movement by a rigid monomer.
source: It is apparent that the transition from the closed to the open state requires relative rearrangements of every GyrA domain and not a unidirectional movement by a rigid monomer.
evidence: This is a conclusion from structural comparisons.

claim: The DNA in the Dihedral complex is well defined and forms a B-DNA double helix that threads through the openings in the four dimers forming the complex.
source: The DNA in the Dihedral complex is well defined and forms a B-DNA double helix that threads through the openings in the four dimers forming the complex.
evidence: This describes the DNA structure observed in the complex.

claim: The T-segment DNA is not perfectly straight, but instead it curves as it passes through the dimers guided by the gate openings and positively charged lysines and arginines in WHD, tower and C-gate domains.
source: The T-segment DNA is not perfectly straight, but instead it curves as it passes through the dimers guided by the gate openings and positively charged lysines and arginines in WHD, tower and C-gate domains.
evidence: This describes the DNA conformation and protein-DNA interactions.

claim: The DNA interacts primarily with three regions in the protein dimer: positively charged patches formed by lysines and arginines in both the WHD and tower domains, a positively charged patch near the C-gate, and the arginines in the neighborhood of the catalytic tyrosine near the DNA-gate.
source: The DNA interacts primarily with three regions in the protein dimer, positively charged patches formed by lysines and arginines in both the WHD and tower domains, a positively charged patch near the C-gate, and the arginines in the neighborhood of the catalytic tyrosine near the DNA-gate. (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes the protein-DNA interactions observed in the structure.

claim: In two of the four dimers the DNA passes through the subunits in an identical manner, resulting in two types of GyrA-ΔCTD/DNA interactions in the oligomer.
source: In two of the four dimers the DNA passes through the subunits in an identical manner, resulting in two types of GyrA-ΔCTD/DNA interactions in the oligomer (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes the two distinct DNA-protein interaction modes.

claim: The positioning of the DNA mimics a T-segment in two distinct states during the strand passage (State A and State B).
source: The positioning of the DNA mimics a T-segment in two distinct states during the strand passage (State A and State B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: In State A the DNA interacts with arginines and lysines in the WHD and C-gate domains.
source: In State A the DNA interacts with arginines and lysines in the WHD and C-gate domains, while in State B, DNA interacts with WHD and tower domains.
evidence: This describes the specific protein-DNA interactions in State A.

claim: In State B, DNA interacts with WHD and tower domains.
source: In State A the DNA interacts with arginines and lysines in the WHD and C-gate domains, while in State B, DNA interacts with WHD and tower domains.
evidence: This describes the specific protein-DNA interactions in State B.

claim: These DNA-interacting regions are highly conserved, suggesting a universal mode of DNA interaction among all gyrases.
source: These DNA-interacting regions are highly conserved (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting a universal mode of DNA interaction among all gyrases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on sequence conservation analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Modeling of a G-segment on the open complex shows that the T-segment DNA in State A aligns with the G-segment DNA with an approximately 82° angle.
source: Modeling of a G-segment on the open complex shows that the T-segment DNA in State A aligns with the G-segment DNA with an approximately 82° angle and the DNA in State B forms an approximately 64° angle with the G-segment DNA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from modeling studies.

claim: The DNA in State B forms an approximately 64° angle with the G-segment DNA.
source: Modeling of a G-segment on the open complex shows that the T-segment DNA in State A aligns with the G-segment DNA with an approximately 82° angle and the DNA in State B forms an approximately 64° angle with the G-segment DNA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from modeling studies.

claim: These angles are consistent with computational and experimental predictions for the angles between the G- and T-segments that would be formed by a positive supercoil wrap induced by gyrase prior to strand passage (~60°) and for angles between the segments in the relaxation of positive supercoils by Topo IV (~85°).
source: These angles are consistent with computational and experimental predictions for the angles between the G- and T-segments that would be formed by a positive supercoil wrap induced by gyrase prior to strand passage (~60°) (Chen et al., 2018; Stone et al., 2003) and for angles between the segments in the relaxation of positive supercoils by Topo IV (~85°) (Neuman et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement compares the observed angles with prior predictions, supported by citations.

claim: Superposition of the Tetrahedral dimer on the Dihedral dimer with the DNA above the DNA-gate shows that in the Dihedral complex the WHD and tower domains move to maximize the specific interactions with DNA.
source: Superposition of the Tetrahedral dimer on the Dihedral dimer with the DNA above the DNA-gate shows that in the Dihedral complex the WHD and tower domains move to maximize the specific interactions with DNA; the twisting of the domains as they open facilitates this interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from structural comparison.

claim: The DNA in the Tetrahedral complex has an overall toroidal shape, but is differently oriented inside the protein cage.
source: The DNA in two Tetrahedral complex sub-classes analyzed has an overall toroidal shape, but is differently oriented inside the protein cage.
evidence: This describes the DNA structure observed in the Tetrahedral complex.

claim: The location of the T-segment in State B of the Dihedral complex is compatible with the recent structure of a fragment of human topoisomerase II with a G-segment in a (partially) open conformation.
source: The location of the T-segment in State B of the Dihedral complex is also compatible with the recent structure of a fragment of human topoisomerase II with a G-segment in a (partially) open conformation. This assembly corresponds to GyrA-ΔCTD, the C-terminal portion of GyrB, and G-segment DNA (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure, supported by citation.

claim: When the State B open dimer is aligned with the human topoisomerase II/DNA structure, the T-segment DNA from State B fits very well in the groove between the human topoisomerase II A and B subunits.
source: Indeed, when the State B open dimer is aligned with the human topoisomerase II/DNA structure (Chen et al., 2018), (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), the T-segment DNA from State B fits very well in the groove between the human topoisomerase II A and B subunits, as proposed in that study (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a result from structural alignment, supported by citation and figure.

claim: The predicted angle of the T-segment in reference to G-segment DNA is in agreement with the angle of the T-segment observed in State B of the Dihedral complex.
source: Finally, the predicted angle of the T-segment in reference to G-segment DNA (Chen et al., 2018; Neuman et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2003) is in agreement with the angle of the T-segment observed in State B of our Dihedral complex.
evidence: This statement compares the observed angle with prior predictions, supported by citations.

claim: In State B, DNA interacts with conserved positively charged arginines and lysines in the tower and WHD domains in both monomers in an almost symmetrical manner.
source: In State B, DNA interacts with conserved positively charged arginines and lysines in the tower and WHD domains in both monomers in an almost symmetrical manner.
evidence: This describes the protein-DNA interactions in State B.

claim: In State A, DNA interacts with the WHD and C-gate domains in an asymmetric manner.
source: In State A, it interacts with the WHD and C-gate domains in an asymmetric manner.
evidence: This describes the protein-DNA interactions in State A.

claim: The DNA-gate in the GyrA-ΔCTD dimers is open just enough to accommodate the passing strand.
source: The DNA-gate in the GyrA-ΔCTD dimers is open just enough to accommodate the passing strand, so that the positive electrostatic field surrounding the areas above and below the gate remains proximal and may guide passage.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the structural data.

claim: A structure of a human topoisomerase II fragment in complex with G-segment DNA shows a similar, but significantly smaller, opening of the DNA-gate.
source: A structure of a human topoisomerase II fragment in complex with G-segment DNA (Chen et al., 2018) shows a similar, but significantly smaller, opening of the DNA-gate.
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure, supported by citation.

claim: The complex provides confirmation that an open GyrA dimer can accommodate a passing DNA strand during the supercoiling cycle.
source: Furthermore, the complex provides confirmation that an open GyrA dimer can accommodate a passing DNA strand during the supercoiling cycle and predicts which DNA and C-gate residues are involved in charge driven interactions with DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural data.

claim: It is possible that the interactions with the WHD and C-gate domains are coupled; as the DNA passes through the DNA-gate it interacts with the C-gate and triggers the conformational changes that open one gate and close the other.
source: Moreover, it is possible that the interactions with the WHD and C-gate domains are coupled; as the DNA passes through the DNA-gate it interacts with the C-gate and triggers the conformational changes that open one gate and close the other.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The T-segment intermediates were observed in the absence of G-segment or GyrB.
source: It is important to note that we observe T-segment intermediates in the absence of G-segment or GyrB, which may help guide strand passage in the native enzyme.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: The T-segment in the complexes is compatible with other structures, such as the human topoisomerase II/DNA structure that include the G-segment and polypeptide regions equivalent to portions of GyrB.
source: However, the T-segment in our complexes is compatible with other structures, such as the human topoisomerase II/DNA structure (Chen et al., 2018) that include the G-segment and polypeptide regions equivalent to portions of GyrB, supporting our conclusion that the complexes reveal bona fide strand passage intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by comparison with other structures and citation.

claim: The Dihedral and Tetrahedral complexes can coexist when GyrB is included but the Dihedral complex predominates when GyrB is excluded.
source: Importantly, the Dihedral and Tetrahedral complexes can coexist when GyrB is included but the Dihedral complex predominates when GyrB is excluded.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Addition of GyrB and novobiocin promoted formation of the Tetrahedral complex with highly bent, heterogeneous DNA inside the protein cage.
source: Addition of GyrB and novobiocin promoted formation of the Tetrahedral complex with highly bent, heterogeneous DNA inside the protein cage.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: GyrB is not incorporated into the Tetrahedral complex, but must be present in the reaction for complex formation.
source: Although GyrB is not incorporated into the Tetrahedral complex, it must be present in the reaction for complex formation and therefore has a role in complex assembly.
evidence: This is an experimental observation and inference.

claim: In both complexes, the protein subunits are arranged in a symmetrical way where the DNA breaks the symmetry of the complex.
source: Whereas the two structures are different, in both models the protein subunits are arranged in a symmetrical way where the DNA breaks the symmetry of the complex.
evidence: This is an observation about the symmetry of the structures.

claim: The opening of the DNA-gate requires conformational rearrangement of all GyrA domains.
